newsitem.title: USA: Simpson defense offers closing arguments, strategy.
newsitem.headline: Simpson defense offers closing arguments, strategy.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's lead attorney in his wrongful death civil trial laid out the defence strategy for next week's closing arguments on Friday, saying "If you can't trust the messenger, you can't trust the message."

"We are saying the jury should distrust every piece of evidence in this case," attorney Robert Baker told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki, arguing that he should be able to tell the jury that evidence in the wrongful death case was "planted, contaminated and altered."

Fujisaki, despite vigorous objections from attorneys for the plaintiffs, said Baker could use the theories in his closing arguments, although he had not been allowed to bring them up during the evidence portion of the trial.

With the jury absent from court, lawyers from both sides huddled behind closed doors in the morning to work out the instructions Fujisaki will give the jury before it gets the case for deliberations, possibly by next Thursday.
Attorneys then met with the judge in open court in the afternoon to resolve their differences over the instructions.

At the end of the session, plaintiffs' lawyer Daniel Petrocelli, who will give his closing statement on Tuesday, raised an objection to Baker's plan to use the theory of evidence planting and contamination in the defence final summation.
But Fujisaki ruled the defence could argue "as they see fit."

The former American football star, actor and TV pitchman was acquitted in October 1995 of the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, and is battling a lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.

When the judge gives the jury its instructions, the panel will be told that if members find Simpson responsible for the deaths they must also decide the actual damages in the case, including such details as the cost of the victims' funerals and the value of the clothes they wore when they were murdered.

At the same time, they will be asked to decide on compensatory damages for "loss of love, companionship, comfort and affection" for Goldman's father, Fred Goldman, and his mother, Sharon Rufo, who is divorced from the father.

The Brown family did not sue for compensatory damages because it would have meant Simpson's two young children by his ex-wife, Sydney and Justin, testifying against their father about the loss of their mother.

But both families are suing for punitive damages over the pain and suffering the victims experienced while they were being murdered. If Simpson loses the case, the jury will be asked to consider punitive damages after hearing from witnesses about Simpson's finances.
